clinicalPearls: A prodrome of prominent, often severe, gastrointestinal disturbance with diarrhoea and marked weight loss is a highly characteristic early clue.
The triad of gastrointestinal symptoms, central nervous system hyperexcitability and cognitive or psychiatric change points strongly to DPPX.
Central nervous system hyperexcitability manifests as exaggerated startle, myoclonus, tremor, rigidity and hyperekplexia-like features.
There is clinical overlap with the progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM) spectrum.
It is usually non-paraneoplastic, but an association with B-cell neoplasms such as lymphoma is recognised and warrants screening.
Dysautonomia, sleep disturbance and brainstem or cerebellar features may accompany the syndrome.
Because the target regulates a potassium channel, its dysfunction produces neuronal hyperexcitability throughout central and enteric networks.
It is a rare but treatable cause of unexplained weight loss with neurological signs, so early recognition matters.
reference.pathophysiology: Dipeptidyl-peptidase-like protein 6 (DPPX, encoded by DPP6) is an auxiliary, catalytically inactive subunit of the Kv4.2 voltage-gated potassium channel complex that regulates the gating, surface trafficking and kinetics of the somatodendritic A-type potassium current. It is expressed widely in the central nervous system and in the myenteric plexus of the gut. Pathogenic IgG antibodies, predominantly IgG1 and IgG4, bind DPPX and reduce surface levels of the DPPX-Kv4.2 complex, diminishing the A-type potassium current that normally restrains neuronal firing. Loss of this inhibitory current yields widespread neuronal hyperexcitability, accounting for the exaggerated startle, myoclonus, rigidity and seizures centrally, and for enteric neuronal overactivity that produces the prominent diarrhoea and weight loss. The broad anatomical distribution of DPPX explains the combined gastrointestinal, cognitive, psychiatric and hyperexcitability phenotype and its overlap with PERM. Most cases are idiopathic, but a subset arises in association with B-cell lymphoproliferative disorders, implicating aberrant B-cell activity in generating the antibody.
additionalDifferentials: Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus and stiff-person spectrum (including anti-GlyR and anti-GAD)
Coeliac or other enteropathy causing weight loss with neurological features
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and other rapidly progressive dementias
Hereditary or acquired hyperekplexia of other cause
Functional or psychiatric gastrointestinal disorder with anxiety
additionalInvestigations: Serum and cerebrospinal fluid cell-based assay for DPPX IgG
Investigations for B-cell lymphoproliferative disease including cross-sectional imaging and haematological work-up
Electroencephalography and electromyography to characterise hyperexcitability and myoclonus
Gastrointestinal evaluation for chronic diarrhoea and to exclude structural or infective causes
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis with oligoclonal bands and infection exclusion
Autonomic function testing where dysautonomia is prominent
redFlags: Severe unexplained diarrhoea and weight loss preceding neurological decline
Exaggerated startle with rigidity and myoclonus suggesting a PERM-like course
Evidence of an underlying B-cell lymphoma on screening
Autonomic instability or respiratory compromise from severe rigidity
reference.prognosis: The disorder is often responsive to immunotherapy, but relapses occur and recovery can be protracted, with residual hyperexcitability or cognitive symptoms in some. Prognosis is poorer where an associated lymphoproliferative malignancy is present.
pitfalls: Investigating the gastrointestinal prodrome in isolation and missing the neurological association
Overlooking screening for B-cell lymphoproliferative disease
Confusing the presentation with a primary functional gastrointestinal or anxiety disorder
Failing to recognise the PERM-like overlap and its treatment implications
Delaying immunotherapy in a treatable but potentially relapsing condition
references: Autoimmune encephalitis diagnostic and management consensus guidance
management: First-line immunotherapy with corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, escalating to rituximab or cyclophosphamide
Screen for and treat an associated B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder such as lymphoma
Symptomatic suppression of central nervous system hyperexcitability, myoclonus and startle with benzodiazepines
Nutritional support and management of the prominent diarrhoea and weight loss, correcting resultant deficits
Monitor for and manage dysautonomia and progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus overlap features
Maintenance immunotherapy and relapse surveillance with multidisciplinary follow-up
